parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle High German glanz, from Old High German glanz (“brilliance”). Cognate with modern German Glanz.

From the imperative of Middle High German haln (“fetch”), from Old High German holōn, from Proto-West Germanic *holōn. Comparable to modern German hallo, Spanish hola. Popularized via the telephone akin to English hello. Associated via phonetic pattern to hälsning (“greeting”), häll (“hail”).
From Middle High German or Middle Low German jesen, gesen (German gären), from Proto-Germanic *jesaną.
From Old Swedish kesar(e), keysar(e) (“emperor”), from Middle High German keiser, ultimately from Latin Caesar; the cognomen of Julius Caesar.
Borrowed from Middle High German kisel, from Old High German kisil, from Proto-West Germanic *kisil, *kesul (“pebble, gravel”).
Inherited from Old Swedish libbestikka, lybbestikka, from Middle High German lübbestock, from Old High German lubistekkila, from from Proto-West Germanic *lubistik.

parole.significato: a magnet (piece of material that attracts metal by magnetism)
parole.testo: From Middle High German magnet(e), from Latin magnēs, from Ancient Greek μαγνης (magnēs, “Magnesian”).

parole.significato: a marmot (rodent of the genera Marmota)
parole.testo: The last part is djur. Ultimately from Middle High German murmeltier, like Icelandic múrmeldýr, Danish and Norwegian Nynorsk murmeldyr.

parole.significato: to stamp, to dent, to make an impression
parole.testo: From Old Swedish präga, from Middle High German praechen, from Old High German (gi)prāhhan. The l was likely added due to intrusion from prägel.

parole.significato: juice (within an organism – usually a plant, sometimes an animal)
parole.testo: From Middle High German Saft. Related to sav (English sap).

parole.significato: to get, to acquire, to procure
parole.testo: From Old Swedish skaffa, from Middle High German schaffen, from Old High German scaffan (from scepfen, from Proto-West Germanic *skappjan. Cognate with Old Swedish skepja (see Swedish skapa)).

From Middle High German sleier, sleiger, sloiger, slogier. Of uncertain ultimate origin, but most likely borrowed; perhaps related to Latin stragulus (“covering”). Compare Middle Low German sleyer, sloier, sloiger, Middle English scleire, scleyre, sleyre, slyre (“veil”).
Probably from West Germanic influence, Middle High German snëgge, snëcke, from Old High German sneggo, snecco, from Proto-Germanic *sneggô.
From Middle High German strumpf, from Proto-Germanic *strumpaz.

parole.significato: any shrub of the genus Daphne
parole.testo: From Old Swedish tybast, from Middle High German zidelbast.
